content: Naegleria is a free-living amoeba that is commonly found in natural environments, particularly in water and soil. While human infections are rare, they are extremely serious when they occur. To reduce the risk of infection, it is important to take precautions to prevent water from entering the nose during activities such as recreational water sports. Among the various species of Naegleria, only Naegleria fowleri is known to infect humans. Although infections with Naegleria fowleri are exceedingly rare, they are more likely to occur during the summer months when the weather is hot, water temperatures are elevated, and water levels are low. The incidence of infections tends to increase during periods of heat waves. Once symptoms of the infection begin, the disease progresses rapidly, often leading to death within approximately five days, though the range can vary from one to twelve days. Naegleria fowleri causes a condition known as primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), which is a severe brain infection that results in the destruction of brain tissue. In its early stages, the symptoms of PAM may resemble those of bacterial meningitis. Early symptoms include headache, fever, nausea, and vomiting. As the disease progresses, later symptoms may include a stiff neck, confusion, reduced attention to surroundings and people, loss of balance, seizures, and hallucinations. The diagnosis of Naegleria fowleri infection is typically made through the microscopic examination of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). A wet mount of the CSF may reveal motile trophozoites, while a Giemsa-stained smear can show trophozoites with characteristic morphology. Additional diagnostic methods include confocal microscopy, cultivation of the organism, and identification using direct immunofluorescent antibody techniques. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based methods, both conventional and real-time, have also been developed for detecting and identifying free-living amoebic infections in clinical samples. These advanced techniques are generally available in specialized reference diagnostic laboratories. Several drugs have demonstrated effectiveness against Naegleria fowleri in laboratory settings. However, their clinical efficacy remains uncertain, as the vast majority of infections have been fatal even with treatment. Amphotericin B has been successfully used in a small number of cases to treat PAM caused by Naegleria fowleri.
